title: Horn
reference_instrument: University of Iowa MIS French horn (model unstated; performer J. Wiskus)
summary: A stand-in, and mostly not graded: a natural baroque horn in D on a trombone's artificial lip, with no hand in the bell and no valve tubing, beside Iowa's modern horn. A2 scores 5 of 11; A3 and D4 have no count, Db2 has no recording and Db5 doesn't speak. D4 takes about 1.9 s to come up. The bore is the plotted profile of Fig. 7 of Bilbao and Chick (2013, JASA 134), which the authors hand-measured to within 5 %: 114 vertices that we read from the figure's vector data, 4.52 m with the PHC 22 mouthpiece inside the bore, 111 cones on the card. The lip, the 6.22 kPa hold and the microphone are the tenor trombone's (Cullen 2000 Table A.2 embouchure 19, artificial latex lips on a trombone-size mouthpiece, not a horn player's). Every note now blows flat from rest, with no borrowed attack. A3 and D4 sit on the printed D crook (lip settings 0.80 and 1.10, picked from a nine-setting ladder by which bore peak each plays, no recording involved) and are posted for hearing. A2 and Db2 are on crooks of our own arithmetic on that bore, 0.138 m and 0.042 m shorter, solved once from the pitch a first try sounded (52 c and 100 c sharp); they now sound within about 3 c of equal temperament.
physics_present: the generic lip-valve performer, outlet observer and file format used for the tenor trombone, now carrying a whole horn bore as cones: the passive plane-wave maxima of the digitised bore are 64.6, 102.9, 144.3, 181.2, 219.4 and 254.3 Hz against the authors' measured 64.8, 103.7, 144.7, 181.9, 220.3 and 256.2 Hz (all within 13 c)

a flat blow on all four notes: the pressure rises to 6.22 kPa in 0.05 s and stays, with the 12 kPa attack borrowed from the trombone removed, and each note settles on the hold the attack led to (same lip gap and closed share, pitch within 2 c)

flow noise at the lips on all four notes (Oldham and Ukpoho 1990, extrapolated), sized by the blowing pressure and the card's 9.014 mm rim radius with no level set: it brings the held note's harmonic-to-noise ratio near the recording's on A2 and most of the way on A3 and D4, but its floor has no frequency shape, so above 2 kHz it sits 3 to 35 dB over the recording's and the spectral distance doesn't improve
physics_missing: the Iowa horn's own bore: no numeric profile of a modern single or double horn was found; the Edinburgh museum catalogue lists about seven bore diameters at key points of one double horn, and the horn that speaks here is a different instrument (a baroque natural horn), read from a figure
the hand in the bell, which lowers the cutoff and moves the upper resonances on every note (Dell et al. 2015): the paper was not found, so there is no published hand geometry or impedance

rotor and branch-slide tubing for the F and B-flat sides, and a horn mouthpiece measured separately (the baroque card's PHC 22 cup is the first 63 mm of its measured bore, with the lumped cup volume at the format floor)

a lip valve for horn players: the lip is the trombone's artificial one, and on the low notes it swings far outside the opening it was measured at (maximum gap 5.6 to 6.5 mm at A2 and 18 mm at Db2, against a 9 mm wide lip and 1.5 mm at A3)

the pitch the lip settles on: on every steady note the sound is 2.0 to 4.5 Hz above the calculated bore maximum (13 to 30 c at A3 to E4); the engine's own passive maxima agree with a plane-wave sum to 0.6 Hz or better, so it isn't the bore calculation, and the peak's half-width doesn't explain it; the cause is not found

a Db5 that speaks: five lip settings from 0.84 to 0.96 of the calculated maximum start no oscillation at the trombone's 6.22 kPa hold or at 12 kPa, the old card's attack pressure; those settings make the lip 6 to 8 times stiffer than at A3, so a higher pressure is untried

a player's start to the note: from rest on the flat blow A2 is up by about 0.4 s, A3 reaches 90 % of its level by 0.73 s, Db2 speaks from about 1.0 s and D4 is near silent until about 1.5 s, full by 1.9 s; the clips keep those leads
the dips at H3, H5, H8 and H10 on A2, which the recording doesn't have: they're already in the lip's flow, and why the lip makes them hasn't been traced
blocked: No whole numeric bore of a modern horn and no hand-in-bell geometry found in open literature; the baroque horn of Bilbao and Chick (2013) stands in.
